Well, the doctrine of tabula rasa has influenced our understanding of human nature since Enlightenment-era empiricism. Philosophers like John Locke believed that humans learned their behavioral traits through experience. So, most psychologists in the twentieth century went into the field with that assumption in their head. It wasn't until the cognitive revolution that psychologists became confident enough in their ability to study the mind to question the doctrine.

The history of science teaches us that common sense is often wrong. In the absense of verifiable evidence, psychologists assumed that sex differences in cognition were inculcated, not because that is "common sense" because it is the least subject to bias. Psychologists were afraid that they would be hindering people from reaching their potential if they pigeon-holed them into distinct roles. It was a necessary step, really. Psychologists were able to control the culture variable and can now determine which sex differences are innate and which are not with greater ease.
